say: Good morning, inquirers! Today we are shape builders. We will cut circles into pieces, hunt for hidden squares and triangles, count cubes we cannot even see, and fold flat paper into a cube.
The secret for every puzzle today: count in order, so nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice.
I will show you something from home. Make its shape with your hands: a cube, a cuboid, a cylinder or a cone. Then we say its name together.
Before we cut: if I cut a circle in half, and then cut one half in half again, how many pieces will I have? What will they look like?
stuck: Stuck folding: fold the circle so the edges match exactly, then press the fold flat.
Not sure of a name: “Count the straight sides. One straight side: half circle. Two straight sides: quarter circle.”
Finished early: find 3 different ways to make a whole circle from your pieces.

say: “To name a piece I count its straight sides. One straight side and one curved side: a half circle. Two straight sides that meet at a square corner, and one curved side: a quarter circle. Turning it round does not change its name.”
“Squares hide inside bigger squares. I count by size: 1 by 1 first, then I slide a 2 by 2 window and count the places it fits, then 3 by 3. Then I add them up.”
“For cubes I count layer by layer. Cubes cannot float, so if I see a cube on top, there must be a cube under it, even if I cannot see it.”

do: Ask: “How many straight sides does it have? So what is it called?”
Ask: “Where else can your window fit? Have you tried every place?”
Ask: “What is holding up that top cube?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Count one kind or one size at a time, and tick each one.”
Hint 2: “Build it with cubes, or cut out the net and fold it.”
Hint 3: “For a net, pick a bottom square and fold the others up one at a time.”

do: Ask: “How many straight sides does it have? So what is it called?”
Ask: “Where else can your window fit? Have you tried every place?”
Ask: “What is holding up that top cube?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Count one kind or one size at a time, and tick each one.”
Hint 2: “Build it with cubes, or cut out the net and fold it.”
Hint 3: “For a net, pick a bottom square and fold the others up one at a time.”

say: “How can you be sure you counted every cube in a stack, even the ones you cannot see?”
ask: “How can you be sure you counted every cube in a stack, even the ones you cannot see?”
Count layer by layer; every cube on top sits on a cube below, so the hidden ones must be there.

say: “You named pieces by their sides, counted in order and folded nets in your head. That is real shape building.”

p2l8-title.note: Objective: Name and describe half circles and quarter circles and use them to make and break up shapes; count every square and triangle in a figure by working in order; count the cubes in a stack, including hidden ones, layer by layer; decide which nets fold into a cube and find opposite faces. Materials: paper circles (2 per child), scissors, about 12 linking cubes per child (or sugar cubes), the cube-net cut-out page (nets A to F, near the back of the workbook, cut out before the lesson), mini whiteboards. Online: children cut paper circles and build stacks on camera; the tutor shows the stacks and nets on the slides; a cereal box cut open shows a net. No linking cubes at home? Use sugar cubes, dice or small boxes, or draw each stack layer by layer. Time plan: opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6, warm-up 6 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 23.5, mini-lesson 23.5 to 35.5, brain break 35.5 to 38.5, worksheet page 1 38.5 to 52.5, check together, page 1 52.5 to 55, short teaching 55 to 59.5, worksheet page 2 59.5 to 71, check together, page 2 71 to 73.5, flex (spare time) 73.5 to 76.5, talk time 76.5 to 81.5, exit ticket 81.5 to 86.5, looking back 86.5 to 88.5, closing and stamps 88.5 to 90. The Think harder and Go further slides are optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Kit ready at minute 0: ask families to put every item on the desk before the lesson starts (a 30-second check at the start).

p2l8-precheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6. Sneak-peek puzzles: two puzzles on the key idea of today, which the children have NOT learnt yet. Say out loud (about 28 words): "Two sneak-peek puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, so is I do not know. Nobody is marked. Say your answer together on three." Question 1 is an access question: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win (about 45 seconds). Question 2 is the thinking question (about 90 seconds). Then about 2 minutes for the answers slide and the move on. Answers are PRIVATE: each child writes on their own paper and says the answer together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not raise whiteboards together, do not read answers out, do not name children. Q1 answer: 12 cubes (6 in each layer, 2 layers). Listen for: Counting one layer first, then doubling, is a good method. This is a first win for everyone. Q2 answer: 5 (each half circle is 2 quarters: 2 + 2 + 1). Listen for: Listen for "a half circle is half of a circle, which is 2 quarters". Drawing the pieces and cutting them is fine. At the end click to show the answers as "one way to think about it", without saying who had what. Ask only for volunteers: "Would anyone like to tell us how they started?" Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Children can move either way at any time. Everyone joins explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.

p2l8-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Point to one object at a time: "What solid is it the same shape as?" Children make the shape with their hands (fists together for a cube, a long box shape for a cuboid, a tube for a cylinder, hands meeting in a point for a cone), then say the name. Click to show (clicks go dice, tissue box, tin can, party hat: four solids only; the drum and the traffic cone are spare). Ask: "How do you know it is a cube and not a cuboid?" (all 6 faces are the same square). "Which ones can roll?" (cylinder and cone). "Which can you stack?" (cube, cuboid, cylinder standing up). Watch for children who call the cube a square: a square is flat, a cube is a solid with 6 square faces. A game of about 2.5 minutes: stop it on the clock even if the game is not finished.

p2l8-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 10.5. Read each question aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click. Answers: 1) 6 2) a half circle. Spare questions in the guide table: a cylinder has 2 flat faces; 4 quarter circles make 1 whole circle; a cone has a tip and can roll. For 1, hold up a cube and count the faces with the children, putting a finger on each: front, back, left, right, top, bottom. Ask: "How do you know you did not count a face twice?" (go in pairs: front and back, left and right, top and bottom). Ask quick questions 1 and 3 only (about 2 minutes): children answer by thumbs, hands, not by naming a child. The other questions are spare.

p2l8-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 19.5. The two paper circles are cut out BEFORE the lesson (parents cut them; kit at minute 0). Pair work is 5.5 minutes. One circle gives 2 half circles; the other gives 4 quarter circles. Children then put pieces together: whole straight sides must touch. Things to make: a whole circle in different ways, a half circle from 2 quarter circles, a "fan", a "wave" (two half circles side by side, one turned over). Online: the same on camera. Go further (a second what-if, so nobody waits) is the box at the foot of this slide; the question is also posted in the chat when the pairs go to their breakout rooms. It is for ANY child who finishes the explore task or wants more: say it to the whole group as a choice, never as a prize, and never name who tries it. Pairs stay together unless both children agree to split. Answer: 7 quarter circles in all: 1 whole circle (4 quarters) and 3 quarters left over. Take it at the debrief only if a pair offers it.

p2l8-explore2.note: Minutes 19.5 to 23.5. Let pairs keep building, then gather them. Answers: 1) 2. 2) 2 half circles; 4 quarter circles; 1 half circle and 2 quarter circles. 3) 2 straight sides, and yes, they are the same length (each goes from the middle of the circle to its edge). They meet at a square corner. Ask: "What fraction of the circle is a half circle? A quarter circle?" (1/2 and 1/4: last lesson!). Keep it moving (about 4 minutes in all): ask "how do you know?" on question 2 only; about 15 seconds of talk on the other questions.

p2l8-teach1.note: Minutes 23.5 to 25.5. Teach. Hold up a paper circle. Click 1: fold and cut through the middle. "Each half is a half circle (some people call it a semicircle). How many sides? One straight side, one curved side." Click 2: cut one half circle again: "Each piece is a quarter of the circle: a quarter circle. Two straight sides and one curved side." Click 3: put the two straight sides of a quarter circle against a ruler: the same length, and they make a square corner like the corner of a page. Think-aloud: "To name a piece I count its straight sides and look for a curved side. One straight and one curved: half circle. Two straight that meet at a square corner, and one curved: quarter circle."

p2l8-we1.note: Minutes 25.5 to 28.5. Click to reveal each step. Think-aloud: "I count one kind of piece at a time and tick it, so I never miss one or count one twice. The cap has one straight side along the bottom and a curved side: a half circle. The grass pieces each have two straight sides meeting in a square corner and a curved side: quarter circles, even though they face different ways. The stem has 4 straight sides, all the same: a square." Ask: "Does turning a quarter circle make it a different shape?" No. This is the same thinking as the robot on the worksheet.

p2l8-try1.note: Minutes 28.5 to 30. Whiteboards, then click. a) 2. b) 2 half circles make 1 circle and 4 quarter circles make another: 2 circles. Push: "What if he had 1 half circle and 2 quarter circles?" (1 circle). (Item c, what fraction is a quarter circle, is dropped: it is in the explore debrief.)

p2l8-we2.note: Minutes 30 to 33. Click to reveal each step; ask the group to predict before each click. Step 2: hold up a paper 2 by 2 window and slide it: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right. "Can it go anywhere else?" No: 4 places. Think-aloud: "Squares hide inside bigger squares, so I count by size. 1 by 1: 9. 2 by 2: I slide my window: 4. 3 by 3: just the whole grid: 1. 9 + 4 + 1 = 14." Watch for children who count 2 small squares side by side: that is a rectangle, not a square. Ask: "What do you notice about 9, 4 and 1?" (3 + 3 + 3, 2 + 2, 1: the window fits in fewer places as it grows).

p2l8-try2.note: Minutes 33 to 34.5. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) 4 + 1 = 5. b) 6 small + 2 squares made of 4 (the 2 by 2 window fits in 2 places) = 8. There is no 3 by 3 square: the grid is only 2 high. Ask a child to show the window sliding along b. (Item c is dropped: worksheet Q2 has the same type.)

p2l8-key.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Counting only the small squares in Q2a (16 instead of 30): ask "Are there bigger squares hiding?" (2) Calling a quarter circle a half circle when it is turned (Q1): count its straight sides. (3) Counting only the cubes you can see in Q3: ask "What is holding up the top cube?" (4) Thinking any 6 joined squares fold into a cube (Q4).

p2l8-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 38.5. Three minutes: two of movement, one for a drink of water. Call the shapes faster and faster. Add "quarter circle" (one arm up, one arm out to the side, then sweep the hand round). Online: children stay in view of the camera.

p2l8-ws1.note: Minutes 38.5 to 52.5. Pairs work together. Ask "How do you know you have them all?" before giving any help. For Q2a, give pairs a paper window to slide (cut a 2 by 2 and a 3 by 3 hole in card). Q1(c) and Q2(b) (triangles) are marked ★ take-home on the page: children do them at home. Say once, to everyone: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never say who is on which page. Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Pairs are not split unless both children agree.

p2l8-ws1ans.note: Minutes 52.5 to 55. Click each answer after a pair explains theirs (answer lines only). Q1(c) and Q2(b) are take-home stars: the answers stay here so children can mark them at home. Q1c: think in quarter circles: 3 half circles are 6 quarter circles, plus 6 more is 12 quarter circles, and 4 make a circle: 3 circles. Or: 2 half circles make 1 circle, 4 quarter circles make 1 circle, and the last half circle with the last 2 quarter circles make 1 more. Q1: the ears and the feet are half circles; the shoulders are quarter circles; the hat and the hands are triangles. Q2a: the 2 by 2 window fits 3 across and 3 down (9 places), the 3 by 3 window fits in 4 places. Q2b: on the bottom line: 3 single parts, 2 made of 2 parts, 1 whole = 6; on the line across: the same, 6.

p2l8-teachcube.note: Minutes 55 to 57.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 counts the cubes in three stacks). Build this stack with real cubes first, then show the picture. Ask: "How many cubes can you see? How many are there really?" Many children say 6 or 7. Click 1: the top layer. Click 2: the bottom layer: point to the right side, where you can see the end of the back row. Click 3: the stack taken apart. Think-aloud: "I count layer by layer. The top layer has 3. The bottom layer is a rectangle 3 long and 2 deep: 6. Cubes cannot float, so there must be cubes under the top ones. 3 + 6 = 9." On the worksheet the rule is the same: every cube sits on the table or on another cube, and the stack is only as deep as the picture shows (Stack A is only 1 cube deep).

p2l8-teachnet.note: Minutes 57.5 to 59.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 asks which nets fold into a cube; the children cut out and fold nets A to D with the tutor on camera for net A; nets E and F are Think harder 3). Have a printed copy of this net cut out, or open up a small box. Click 1 and 2: fold it in front of the children. Think-aloud: "I choose a bottom. The squares touching it fold up as walls. The row of 4 wraps round: bottom, wall, top, wall. The two loose squares close the ends. Every square lands on a different face, so it is a cube." Click 4: the shape with two squares under the ends: "When I fold, both of these land on the same face. One face gets two squares, and one face gets none. Not a cube." Tip for the worksheet: squares that land on the same place, or a row of 5 or more squares, or a 2 by 2 block of squares mean it is not a cube net.

p2l8-ws2.note: Minutes 59.5 to 71. Children work alone. Q4(b) (add one square to make a cube net) is marked ★ take-home on the page: children do it at home. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Q4 uses the cut-out nets A to D from the kit page (E and F are Think harder 3) at the back of the workbook: parents cut them out BEFORE the lesson (kit at minute 0; if not, give 2 minutes to cut). They decide first, then fold to check. Tutor rule at minute 59.5: if the clock is more than 2 minutes late, drop the last Core question of page 2 to take-home (children draw a star beside it). Never shorten talk time, the exit ticket, looking back or the closing. Questions marked with a star and the words take-home on the page are done at home; their answers are still on the check-together slide.

p2l8-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 73.5. Click each answer after a child explains (answer lines only). Q4(b) is a take-home star: the answer stays here so children can mark it at home. Q3 B: one cube is completely hidden at the back, bottom, left. C: count layers: 9 + 4 + 1 = 14. b) a 3 by 3 by 3 cube has 3 layers of 9: 27; 27 − 14 = 13. Q4a: B (2 by 3) has a 2 by 2 block; D has two squares that land on the same face. (Think harder 3: E folds into a cube; F has a row of 5, which wraps round onto itself.) Q4b: the extra square must go under the row (any of the 4 places), so the two loose squares become the top and the bottom. Above the row, or at the ends, it does not work. The dice net (opposite faces add up to 7) is on the Go further page: in a straight row, the 1st and 3rd squares are opposite, and so are the 2nd and 4th.

p2l8-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Open to any child who chooses it (the choice after question 3 on the worksheet). These are the SAME four questions as the printed Think harder page: the slide shows 1 to 3 and question 4 is on the page only. Never announce who is working on which page. Answers: 1) 19 (12 + 6 + 1) 2) 9: four small squares (1 by 1), two long ones (1 high and 2 long), two tall ones (2 high and 1 long), and the whole grid (2 by 2). 4 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9. 3) E folds into a cube (it is a staircase of squares, one of the 11 cube nets). F does not: the row of 5 squares wraps round and the 1st and 5th squares land on the same face. 4) (Question: Six squares are joined in a straight line. Can they fold into a cube? Explain.) No. When you fold the line round, the 5th square lands on the same face as the 1st and the 6th on the 2nd, and the two ends are left open.

p2l8-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use as a pair go-further or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. More are in the question bank. Answers: 1) 18 cubes. 2) 20 squares in the 4 by 3 grid; the other grid is 7 long and 2 high (14 + 6 = 20). So 4 by 3 and 7 by 2.

p2l8-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The diagrams show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Can you build it? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p2l8-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use after pairs have tried. Q1: you could also count front to back: each slice from the front is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 cubes, and there are 3 slices: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Two ways, same answer: a great check. Q2: the grid is only 3 high, so there is no 4 by 4 square. Watch for 12 (only small squares) and for 21 or more (counting a 4 by 4 that is not there).

p2l8-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then two volunteers share. Listen for: count layer by layer; every cube on top must sit on a cube below (cubes do not float); a layer is a rectangle, so count its rows; build it to check. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Talk time rules: you choose volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"); never cold-call a child by name; any child may say pass; no public tallies, scores or rankings.

p2l8-exit.note: Minutes 81.5 to 86.5. Answer: 7 (bottom layer 3 + 3 = 6, top layer 1). Children who write 4 counted only the front faces and the top cube; ask "What is under the top cube? What is behind the front row?" Extension: How many more cubes would make the stack 2 layers of 6? (5 more). Children keep slips on their desks and tick them against the answer on the next click; nothing is held up. About 2 minutes of child work.

p2l8-reflect.note: Minutes 86.5 to 88.5. Looking back: about 2 minutes, in the box on the page called "Before you go: Investigation and Looking back" (the page after worksheet page 2; every child reaches it). Children finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped. A pass is always allowed. No marks and no wrong answers. Tutor script: SAY: Looking back takes 2 minutes. Find the box called Looking back on the page “Before you go: Investigation and Looking back”. Finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped you. You may pass on any line. If you tick "I am still stuck", your tutor will check in during the session. DO: Nothing is collected in front of the group and nobody has to read theirs out. The tutor may read a box while stamping journals (never by private message), and checks in on a child who ticked still stuck during the open session, for example by a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal with a parent nearby, for example "I saw you drew it when you got stuck". A child may volunteer one sentence, never by name unless they choose to. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the next open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby). Praise the strategy, not the speed. Closing and stamps take the last minute and a half (88.5 to 90).
